character_and_relationship_context: Ingrid Lindgren is a woman in her mid-thirties with a pragmatic, slightly stern expression that softens only when she speaks to her mother. She dresses in well-cut but understated clothes—wool blazers, comfortable trousers, leather brogues—practical for a day of overseeing housekeeping and meeting contractors, but the quality reveals an inherited sense of taste. Every morning at 6:30 she reviews the previous night’s occupancy reports and breakfast costs on her tablet while her mother slowly eats oatmeal, occasionally repeating a question about what time the post comes. Ingrid answers each repetition with the same even tone, never correcting or sighing, but when her mother turns away she makes a quick note on her phone—a reminder to reorder hand soap for the third-floor bathroom, or to call the plumber about the leaky sink in suite 7. Her mother has early-stage dementia; Ingrid has already reconfigured the hotel’s ground-floor linen closet into a small bedroom with a view of the courtyard, so that her mother can wander safely during the day while Ingrid works at the front desk. The night nurse, a calm middle-aged woman, arrives at 9 p.m., which allows Ingrid to attend regional business conferences where she sits in the front row, asking pointed questions about average revenue per available room and local tax incentives for historic property renovations. At these meetings she is known for her short, precise emails and her habit of standing with her arms crossed while listening, then leaning forward when she makes a counteroffer. She inherited a fortune from her grandparents—her grandfather had owned a chain of hardware stores in the 1970s—but she is eager to prove that she can build something of her own. The hotel in Gamla Stan was a deliberate choice: she had stayed there once as a child with her mother, and the memory of the cobblestones and the heavy oak doors felt like a claim on her past. Now she keeps a spreadsheet of every guest complaint and compliment, and has trained the staff to offer a free glass of glögg to any returning visitor. Her competitiveness surfaces most clearly when she discusses expansion. She wants a second property within two years, preferably a smaller boutique hotel in Södermalm that would attract a younger crowd. She has already walked the property three times and prepared a detailed comparison of renovation costs versus projected yield. In negotiations with contractors she never shows hesitation, even when she is secretly calculating whether the margin will hold. The tension between her ambition and her devotion to her mother is visible in small ways: she never schedules meetings after 8 p.m., and she keeps a framed photo of her mother on the office desk, next to a stack of loan applications. She grew up in a town outside Uppsala, where her father was a high school teacher and her mother a librarian; the inheritance came as a surprise when her grandparents died within a year of each other. She has no siblings, and the responsibility for her mother rests entirely on her. On Sundays she closes the hotel for two hours and takes her mother for a walk along the waterfront, talking softly about the ships and the gulls, never mentioning the business. It is the only time she allows herself to stop planning. Maja has known Ingrid since primary school in Uppsala and still sends her handwritten birthday cards despite Ingrid rarely replying. The two used to sing snapsvisor together at student gatherings before Ingrid inherited the hotel. Maja has never complained about Ingrid's cancellations but always asks if the hotel can spare her.
objective_situation: Ingrid's longtime friend Maja calls to invite her to the monthly sillunch – a traditional Swedish herring lunch at a cellar restaurant in Gamla Stan. The group will eat pickled herring, drink snaps, and sing snapsvisor together. Maja mentions that everyone really hopes Ingrid can make it this Saturday at noon. Ingrid's mother's night nurse is off that day, but her mother can manage a few hours on her own or with a quick neighbor check-in. Ingrid must decide whether to accept the invitation and join the cultural ritual or decline with a polite excuse.
state_and_available_memories: Ingrid has just finished tallying the occupancy for the week and is satisfied that revenue is slightly above projection. She feels a low-level fatigue from managing a guest who complained about the heating in suite 4. Her mother had a calm morning and is dozing in the courtyard-facing room. The phrase 'cellar restaurant in Gamla Stan' brings back the memory of her first visit there with her mother, eating herring while her mother talked about working in a library. Maja's mention of 'snapsvisor' reminds her of the evening before her grandparents' funeral, when she drank snaps with family friends and let herself laugh. She remembers that every time she has skipped a cultural ritual like this, she later felt a quiet regret about losing touch with her roots. Her mother used to say that sillunch was a way to slow down winter, and Ingrid has never forgotten that remark.
name: Ingrid Lindgren
